the-case-each-submission-met.text: A command meets one of seven cases for each transaction it submits, read from the latest phase the journal holds for it: acknowledged, when the node accepted it but it was not yet seen on chain; unknown, when no answer arrived; rejected, when the node refused it; included, when it is on chain; timeout, when the confirmation deadline passed; rolled back, when the chain had included it and no longer does; and excluded, when it is off the chain and its validity window has closed, so it can never land.

The table pairs each case with its phase in the journal and with what you do next. For most cases the answer is the same: run your next command, which picks the transaction up from the chain. A rejected or excluded transaction is settled. A rejected one you correct and run again, and an excluded update you simply run again; but when the rejected or excluded transaction is the fold of an insert or a terminate, its booked request stays pending, as the section on transactions that can never land explains. A transaction is prepared once and never sent twice.

the-next-command-reconciles.text: After an inclusion a write commits locally in a fixed order: the proof mirror, then state dot json, then the observed line. Each file is replaced whole or not at all, so an interruption leaves the old version or the new one.

The diagram follows the next command. It checks the saved body against its prepared line and looks for the transaction's first output on chain. If it is there, the transaction is journalled confirmed; the fold's edge is applied to the mirror only from its recorded root before, and only when the ledger already holds its recorded root after; state dot json follows the mirror; and the after-state is read back and journalled observed, for whichever key the interrupted step concerned. Then the command proceeds. If the chain shows nothing, a write stops before building anything and names the transaction and its case.
The receipt says what the reconciliation did, rollbacks and exclusions included. Inspect reconciles only when no other process is writing to the registry.

when-the-chain-rolls-back.text: A transaction the journal saw included can leave the chain again. The next command checks each one: if its first output is gone and an input it spends is live again, it is no longer on the chain, because a transaction on the chain has consumed every input it spends. The command appends a rolled back line naming the chain point it read and the live inputs. The observed line stays where it was.

The diagram follows that check. For a fold, the mirror is rebuilt to the root the fold started from, by replaying from the empty trie the edges of the folds still on the chain, and state dot json follows. The transaction is unresolved again and is never sent again. If the chain includes it again it is reconciled as before; otherwise every write stops on it and names the case rolled back.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: Once the chain's tip has reached the end of a transaction's validity window, and an input it spends is still live, it can never be included. The next command journals it excluded, with the chain point and the live inputs. No later command stops on it, and the write that excluded it proceeds from the root the mirror already holds.

What it leaves on chain depends on the command. An excluded update leaves nothing, so you run it again. But the fold of an insert or a terminate follows a booking that is on chain, and its request stays pending with its deposit. These commands cannot fold or retract it, and while it is pending every later insert or terminate on the registry is refused as a concurrent writer; rerunning books a second deposit and is refused the same way. Updates and inspect still run. Releasing the request needs a tool outside these commands.

Folds carry an upper bound on their window. Bookings and the publications create makes carry none, so a booking that never landed, or one rolled back and not included again, stays unresolved and every write stops on it. That is a known limit of these commands.

when-the-next-command-stops.text: A write that cannot reconcile a transaction stops before building or submitting anything, names the transaction and its case, and leaves the journal as it was. If the chain does not show the transaction yet, or no longer shows it, wait and run the command again: it is reconciled if it lands, and excluded once its window closes without it, leaving, for an insert or terminate fold, the pending request described above. If it is on chain but its edge does not reach the ledger's root, the outcome is stale state and the local files are not repaired. Inspect names the same transaction and case.

what-the-checks-show.text: The recovery controls run each case as separate processes on one development node, and judge every clause from receipts, the journal, the saved bodies and the files, and, for exclusion and rollback, from the node's own answers rather than the command under test.

The table walks the eight controls: an accepting insert; a lost answer, reconciled once by the next insert; a kill before the mirror is saved, after the mirror, and after state dot json, each finished by the next write; a fold never sent, excluded once the tip passed its upper bound so the next write proceeds; a booking never sent, on which the next write stops; and a rollback, made by restarting the node on an earlier copy of its database, after which the command journals both transactions rolled back, returns the local files to the root before, and the next write stops naming the booking.

The rollback is a mechanism of the generated development node, not a fork of a public chain. Every transaction has exactly one prepared line, and nothing written is ever rewritten. Durability across a power loss is not shown, only across a killed process.
